comparison: Perfect agreement on claims C3, C4, C20, C28, C29, C63, C64, C106 regarding random connectivity being sufficient for grouped convergence. Both evaluations find the analytical calculations and simulations provide solid support, with reviewers praising the 'back-of-envelope reasoning' and biological plausibility.

Perfect agreement on claims C103, C104, C105 regarding integration of multiple selectivity forms across timescales. Both evaluations support the multi-scale approach, with reviewers explicitly endorsing this as 'a timely reminder that synaptic clusters and sequences can exist on multiple spatial and temporal scales.'

Strong agreement on claims C5, C30, C73, C74 regarding sequential convergence requiring greater redundancy. Peer review also includes C75, C76 (gap-fills), which OpenEval addresses separately in R18. Both evaluations support the findings as providing 'valuable quantitative insights.'

Agreement on claims C6, C22, C40, C71 regarding nonlinearity requirements for discrimination. Peer review additionally includes C41, C42, C57 (structural insufficiency claims that OpenEval groups in R4). Both evaluations appreciate the transparent reporting of conditions that hinder clustering.

Agreement on claims C44, C45, C48, C51 regarding noise effects and functional roles of different mechanisms. Peer review R4 covers broader multi-scale analysis including C43, C46, C52, C53 (which OpenEval addresses in R4 and R8). Reviewers specifically praise the chemical signaling simulations as 'unique in this area.'

Partial overlap on claims C41, C42, C57 regarding structural connectivity insufficiency. OpenEval R4 also includes C7, C43, C102 (broader synthesis), while peer R3 includes C6, C22, C40, C71 (nonlinearity effects). Both evaluations support the finding that connectivity alone is insufficient.

Agreement on claims C54, C55, C56, C58, C96, C99 regarding network-level simulations and selectivity. Peer review additionally includes C100, C101, C102 (noise and EI balance). Both evaluations accept the balanced assessment including weak somatic selectivity results.

Agreement on claims C81-C85 regarding bistable-switch model simulations. Peer R6 covers broader chemical signaling results including C27, C86-C92 (which OpenEval addresses in R5 and R11). Reviewers praise these simulations as 'unique in this area.'

Agreement on claims C86-C92 regarding Branco model simulations of ectopic effects. Peer R6 also includes C27, C81-C85 (which OpenEval addresses in R5 and R10). Both evaluations support the detailed mechanistic findings on chemical signaling.

Agreement on claims C38, C39 regarding selectivity type distributions. Peer R8 additionally includes C72 (nonlinearity limitations that OpenEval groups in R3). Both evaluations support the nuanced selectivity findings through comprehensive analysis.

Agreement on claims C32, C33, C109-C112, C114 regarding olfactory system applications. Peer R7 also includes C115, C116 (testable predictions that OpenEval evaluates separately as UNCERTAIN in R15). Both evaluations support the application of the analytical framework to specific circuits.

Agreement on claims C107, C108 regarding synthesis conclusions about random connectivity sufficiency. OpenEval R26 also includes C21 (general conclusion). Both evaluations support the main conclusion, with reviewers praising the finding that clustering can occur 'by chance.'

Minimal overlap on claim C27 regarding spatial clustering effects. OpenEval evaluates this single claim separately, while peer R6 groups it with extensive chemical signaling results (C81-C92). Both evaluations support the computational model results.

Partial overlap on claims C46, C52, C53 regarding ectopic input effects. OpenEval focuses on comparative simulations (Figures 5-6), while peer R4 addresses broader multi-scale analysis including C43-C45, C48, C51. Both evaluations support the robustness findings.

Agreement on claims C100, C101 regarding noise level importance. OpenEval evaluates these separately, while peer R5 groups them with broader network-level results (C54-C58, C96, C99, C102). Both evaluations support the dramatic noise effects.

Divergence on claims C115, C116 regarding testable predictions. OpenEval rates these as UNCERTAIN due to lack of experimental validation, while peer review implicitly supports them as part of the practical implications. OpenEval is more conservative about untested predictions.

Partial overlap on claims C75, C76 regarding gap-fills in sequential convergence. OpenEval R18 covers broader signal-to-noise analysis (C75-C80), while peer R2 groups these with sequential convergence claims (C5, C30, C73, C74). Both evaluations support the gap-fill findings.
